With the others already headed back, he wasn’t about to miss a rare moment of fun without getting scolded. “C’mon, golden boy,” he muttered. “One more swing.” He slipped after him, trailing just out of view, boots light on cracked tile. Sparks hissed again, bright red against the dim. Wesker slammed a hand to the wall, steadying himself as a dry heave convulsed his frame. For a heartbeat, Jake thought he’d scored the perfect encore — a front-row seat to the bastard finally falling apart. “Subject 06-W,” a voice drawled, grainy and pleased. “Tremors escalating. Cognitive resistance holding. Containment stable. Recommend further application.” A slow scrape of pen followed, then a quiet chuckle. “You seem tense. Didn’t sleep well, did you?” Another pause. Then softer, amused — “Puppet still dances. Strings intact.” Wesker snarled, spine snapping rigid just as another jolt arced through his arm. His roar shattered into a pained yell as he turned and threw a chair at the speaker, sending it crashing to the floor in a shower of sparks and splinters, only for one on the other side of the room to start chuckling in its stead. Jake’s grin froze. His blood ran cold, breath catching. He took one step back — then another. He wasn’t supposed to hear that. The intercom buzzed once more. Then, faintly — Shh-sskt. The scratch of a pen. Jake turned and bolted. Ch 12 – Burn Pattern Jake stumbled through the Fog, shoulders heaving, eyes wide. For once, he didn’t speak. Just stood there on the edge of the firelight, shaking, a bewildered expression on his face. Someone made an offhanded comment he barely heard about taking forever to get out of the trial — a light jab at best, but the humor died long before it landed. Claudette noticed first, rising from her spot. "Jake? Jake what’s wrong?" He didn’t answer right away. His hands were clenched. His mouth opened. Closed again. Then finally, voice raw: "You were right..." The fire seemed to still. Jake’s voice cracked as he stared past the fire, past the people watching him. "It’s not him. This whole time... not really. He’s— he’s not breaking down. You were right. He’s being used. Controlled." Nea stared. Claudette’s lips parted. Meg swore under her breath. Jake’s voice cracked as the rest spilled out, faster now, outrage climbing in ragged bursts. "The Doctor. He was talking to him like he was some kind of experiment. Recording readings. Mocking him like it was all just fun for him... I don’t—" He broke off, running both hands through his hair. "He’s not losing it. He’s being driven into the dirt." For a moment, no one moved. Gabriel’s voice cut in, low but sharp. "Then it’s true." "He’s interfering with the trials. This is dangerous for all of us if it’s allowed to continue. This isn’t about Wesker anymore. It’s about control."" — By the next return, the fire was on the edge of a total fracture. The survivors gathered around the camp in tight knots, voices brittle. The fractures were spreading. Cooperation — the one thing that had kept them alive — was unraveling. Meg jabbed a finger at Claudette. "You keep defending him, you’re no better than he is. You want to risk all of us on some mercy mission?" Claudette’s voice shook, but she held her ground. "I’m saying this isn’t right. If someone can control the killers... this isn’t about sympathy. It’s survival." "Still sounds like pity to me," Jake snapped. "And pity’ll get you killed. You saw what happened last time you tried to get close." "We all did," Nea said, voice low but firm. "That’s why we can’t ignore it." The circle of fire felt smaller than ever, heat swallowed by distrust. Dwight shifted uncomfortably, but Gabriel’s gaze stayed steady, weighing every word. Gabriel finally spoke, his voice quiet but cutting through the tension. "Look, this isn’t about compassion. This is about control." The group stilled, turning toward him. His tone carried weight — factual, undeniable. "If the rules aren’t consistent, if someone else can tamper with the trials, then none of us are safe. It doesn’t matter if you hate him or want to help him. What matters that it can’t be allowed to continue like this. We’ve survived this long because the rules were stable. Predictable. If someone like the Doctor can break those rules, we lose more than just our edge — we lose the entire system." Dwight nodded, relief flickering across his face. Claudette let out a shaky breath. Even Nea looked emboldened. The pragmatists shifted, unease creeping in despite themselves. Gabriel’s voice didn’t waver. "I got a much better look at that cuff last time and it’s definitely tech of some kind. I was pretty sure before but now, I’m positive. I don’t know what powers it, but it’s definitely some kind of hardware. And if it’s hardware, it can fail." "We need to get it off him." Dwight nodded again, firmer this time. "We need to get that cuff off and prove that we won’t be controlled." Jake shifted in place, torn between his disdain for Wesker and the growing dread of what might happen if they did nothing. "I don’t know how you intend to do that. Last time you tried just to see it, he damn near turned you into paste. What are we supposed to do if he turns on us in the middle of trying?" "It needs to be a coordinated effort," Nea leaned in, determination building. "No matter what domain we land in or who we’re grouped with — if he’s there, we all need to agree on what’s happening. If he shows up, we don’t scatter. We act." Meg let out a shaky breath and slowly sank back beside the fire. "Holy shit... we’re actually doing this.
